title: Anchors and Keywords
intro: An anchor is a fixed place you will always find in the same order. A keyword is the one word that stands for a whole point. This sheet helps you pair them: one anchor, one keyword and one picture for each thing you want to keep.
howTo: Choose a route you know well and write its stops in the Anchor column, in order.
Write each item or point in the Point column.
Underline or write the one word that stands for it in the Keyword column. It should be a thing you can see, or something that sounds like one.
In the Picture column, write a few words that describe your big, odd, moving picture.
Cover the Point and Picture columns, say the keywords by walking the anchors, then check.
lines: No. | Anchor (stop)     | Point (what I need) | Keyword     | My picture (a few words)
First check (no peeking) on: ____________   Number right: ____ of ____
Second check on: ____________   Number right: ____ of ____
The picture I will make stranger: ______________________________

examples.title: Worked example: a grocery list
lines: My route: my flat, from the front door to the kitchen
1 | Front door  | Oranges | oranges | Oranges juggling themselves on the doormat
2 | Hall table  | Bread   | bread   | A loaf as a pillow, snoring
3 | Stairs      | Soap    | soap    | Bubbles pouring down every step
4 | Sofa        | Beans   | beans   | A tin of beans wedged between the cushions
5 | Kitchen sink| Fish    | fish    | A fish doing laps in the washing-up water

examples.title: Worked example: a talk of five points
lines: 1 | Door   | Where we are now         | signpost | A signpost swings open in the doorway
2 | Window | What went well           | sun      | A golden sun squeezes in through the glass
3 | Desk   | What did not go well     | cup      | A cracked cup spills over the papers
4 | Shelf  | What we will do next     | toolbox  | A toolbox on the top shelf rattles
5 | Lamp   | What I need from you     | handshake| Two hands shaking under the lamp

honest: Writing it down is only the setup. The memory comes from walking the stops and checking yourself without looking, then again after a gap. A written copy is still your safest copy.

title: My Image Library Builder
intro: An image library is your own set of pictures for numbers. When you have a fixed picture for each pair of digits, long numbers become quick short stories. Build yours a few at a time, and use pictures that mean something to you. Nobody else needs to understand them.
howTo: Start with the sound code. Each digit stands for a sound: 0 is s or z, 1 is t or d, 2 is n, 3 is m, 4 is r, 5 is l, 6 is j, sh or ch, 7 is k or hard g, 8 is f or v, 9 is p or b.
For a pair such as 26, take the sounds n and j (or ch) and add vowels as you like: niche, notch, nacho. Choose one word you can picture clearly.
Choose a person, creature or thing, not a quality. 'Nacho' is easier than 'nice'.
Write your word and a few words describing the picture. Aim for 10 pairs at a time, not all 100 at once.
Test yourself: cover the picture column, say the pair, and see whether the picture comes at once. Replace any that make you pause.
Use pictures that are personal: a friend's pet, a shop you like, a toy from your childhood.
lines: Pair | Sounds     | My word      | My picture (a few words)
(continue the same layout down to 99, ten pairs to a row of ten)
Pairs I check this week: ____ to ____
honest: This is a lot of work for a payoff you only get on numbers, so only build the part you will use. Mnemos already has a place to keep your list (Month 4). Use this sheet to plan it away from the screen. It is for numbers you can share, and never for PINs or passwords.

title: Map a Topic
intro: A Mind Map shows how a topic fits together. Use this sheet to plan one on paper, then to test yourself by redrawing it blank.
howTo: Write your topic in the middle box. Use one to three words.
Write three to six branch names around it. Each is one big part of the topic.
Add two to four leaves to each branch. A leaf is one to three words, not a sentence.
Study the map for a few minutes. Then turn the page over.
Redraw it from memory on a blank page: the middle, the branches, then the leaves.
Compare it with the original. Circle every leaf you missed and every leaf you put under the wrong branch.
honest: The map shows how the topic fits together. The part that helps memory is closing it and rebuilding it from memory. If you only look at your map, you will mostly learn that you have seen it. Facts on your map must be true and checked from a source you trust.

title: Map the People
intro: A profile grid helps you keep a few details about the people you meet, such as the people in a new class, a club or a team. Keep it light and kind. It is for being thoughtful, not for collecting information about anyone.
howTo: Write one person's first name and a feature you noticed in the first row.
Add only details they told you freely and that you would be happy for them to read: where they are from, something they enjoy, a pet's name.
Turn the name into a picture and the detail into a picture. Join them in one scene.
Cover the grid and say what you remember about each person.
Check what you missed and fix those pictures.
lines: Name | Feature I noticed | Where we met | Something they enjoy | My picture
Checked the next morning: ____ of ____ right
Checked a week later: ____ of ____ right
honest: Pictures only help if you paid attention when you met. Many people like to be remembered by name, but we do not claim it changes how anyone treats you. In the game, all the people are invented.

title: Before and After
intro: Do you want to find out whether a method helps you? Try it on your own real material. Write down how you did before you used the method, then how you do after. This is for you, not for proof.
howTo: Choose something real you want to keep, such as a list of ten items or a short talk.
Before you use any method: study it your own way for a set time, then write what you remember, without looking. Write your score.
Wait a day or so. Learn a similar-sized new piece with the method. Study it for the same time.
Write your score for that piece, the same way.
Check both again a week later, and write both scores.
lines: The material before the method: ____________________   How many items: ____
Score the same day (right out of total): ____ of ____
The new material: ____________________   How many items: ____
honest: These are your scores on your own material, nothing more. They do not show that Mnemos or any method works in general.
